title: How Mobile Estimating Changes Shop Operations
summary: Discover how AI-powered mobile estimating improves customer capture, frees estimators, and transforms collision repair shop operations.
body_markdown:
*Mobile estimating changes who can talk to a customer. That has consequences nobody warns you about.*


In this month’s[Run My Business episode](https://youtu.be/Csv_wAjt5iA) , Craig Stevens makes an argument I’ve been chewing on since I first heard it: stop letting the estimating process stall every time somebody steps away from a desk. Watch it. It’s five minutes and he lays out the case better than I can.


What I want to talk about is what happens the week after you agree with him. Because the tool is the easy part. Handing your intake process to somebody who isn’t a twenty-year estimator changes your shop in ways that are worth thinking through before you do it.


## Why This Is Suddenly Urgent


Crash Course 2026 reports scheduling backlogs down to roughly 1.8 weeks, from about 5.8 weeks in early 2023. Sit with that for a second. Three years ago, your problem was too much work and not enough bays. Today the bays are open.


When you had a five-week backlog, a customer who waited twenty minutes in your lobby was an inconvenience you could absorb. With a 1.8-week backlog, that same customer is a job you need to capture. The parking lot stopped being a queue and became a capture point, and most of us haven’t restaffed or retooled for that.


## What It Actually Does to Your Org Chart


Craig’s advice is to put your people with great personalities in front of customers. He’s right, and the implication is bigger than a scheduling tweak.


For as long as any of us have been doing this, the ability to stand in front of a customer and talk about damage and dollars was gated behind years of estimating experience. That gate is what made the job hard to hire for and expensive to fill. When AI writes the preliminary exterior lines, the gate moves.


Three things follow:


- **Your hiring profile widens.** You can hire for temperament and train the software, instead of hunting for a unicorn who has both.
- **Your apprentices get a rung to climb.** Walking a vehicle with a customer is now an entry point, not a graduation. That is a retention tool in a trade that struggles to keep young people.
- **Your senior estimators gain focus for their skills.** Name what those recovered hours are for, whether it's deeper teardowns, supplement prep, or coaching your newer writers. Time that isn't reassigned has a way of refilling itself.


## The Handoff Nobody Talks About


Here is the part that keeps me up, and it’s the honest counterweight to all this enthusiasm.


CCC’s own numbers say Mobile Jumpstart captures over 81% of the estimate total and generates nearly 25 lines, in under 80 seconds. That is genuinely impressive. It also means close to a fifth of that estimate is not there yet, and the missing fifth is exactly where structural discovery, ADAS calibration, and OEM procedures live.


A preliminary estimate written in the parking lot is a starting point, not a repair plan. If your process doesn’t include a hard handoff to a seasoned estimator after teardown, you haven’t moved work off your best people. You’ve just moved where the supplement fight starts.


Write the handoff down. Who owns the file at each stage, what triggers the escalation, and what your CSR is explicitly not authorized to promise a customer standing at the hood.


## Configure It or Don’t Bother


One number that should change how you roll this out: shops running the highest AI permission settings write roughly 60% more AI-generated lines than shops left on the basic defaults.


That is an enormous spread, and it explains why two shops can try the same tool and come away with completely different opinions. If you turn this on, assign somebody to actually tune the settings to your predictions, part codes, your R&I preferences. Otherwise, you will run it at a fraction of its capability and conclude the whole idea was oversold.


## The Numbers Worth Watching


Craig’s advice is to look for the moments where work stops. That’s a good instinct, and here’s how to put some numbers behind it.


Capture rate is where I’d start. It tells you how many of the estimates you wrote actually turned into repair orders, and if moving intake out to the parking lot is working, that’s where you’ll see it first.


Cycle time is the second one, though I’d look at the front end of it rather than the whole keys-to-keys number. How long is it from a vehicle landing on your lot to a repair starting on it? That stretch is where the mobile process either helps you or doesn’t.


Split them by how the vehicle showed up. Walk-ins, tows, and scheduled drop-offs behave nothing alike, and a blended number will quietly hide whichever one you’re losing.


And give yourself a baseline for a couple of weeks first. Otherwise, you won’t know whether mobile intake moved the needle or just moved the bottleneck.


None of this is really about software.


For twenty years I watched the same pattern hold. The person who could stand in front of a customer and talk about damage and dollars had to be the person who’d earned it, one sheet at a time. There wasn’t another option.


Now there is. But a tool doesn’t decide how your shop runs. You do.


Watch Craig’s five minutes with your front-office team at the next morning huddle. Then stay in the room for the harder conversation about the handoff, and about what you’re actually going to do with the hours you just gave your best estimator back.


That conversation decides how you grow and how competitive you become.


Watch “[Start Estimates Anywhere: The Power of CCC Mobile Jumpstart](https://youtu.be/Csv_wAjt5iA) ”.
